Name: Rajratna Adsul
Question: Who is an author known for making difficult topics easy to understand? Can you recommend any of their books that you found particularly enlightening in this aspect?
Answer: Yesterday I bought Susskind's General Relativity in the Theoretical Minimum Series. I ordered the book from Amazon. I had glanced at this book earlier online, but somehow I felt I should buy it to make my bookshelf complete with Susskind's books. This book is so beautifully written that I have no words to describe. Each word of this book carries a ton of knowledge. Read the reviews by some of the established authors. Everytime I take some book on general relativity to read, I find some interesting aspect of the beauty of its theory. This book takes you from scalars, vectors and tensors to Penrose diagrams of Schwarzchild geometry in just 350 pages! Each diagram of the book illuminates a bulk of the theory. Though what I wrote above (Penrose diagrams……) may sound intimidating, the book really cares to teach you general relativity in its basic form. The style, layout, diagrams are so clean and clear that one doesn't need much outside help to understand the content. The book was released in 2022 for Rs 2000 then. I was bit disappointed to see it overpriced at that time. I got its pdf copy but couldn't read the book due to busy schedule. Now it's 2024 and the price dropped to Rs 450! As I was already familiar with Susskind's books on other topics, I thought I better complete his series with this addition. If a book like this one teaches you Christoffel symbols and hyperbolic coordinates with such ease and comfort, then I'm fortunate to have such great minds like Leonard Susskind around to write with great wit and clarity on such a difficult subject as general relativity!

Question: Can a person who has little knowledge about something accurately estimate the level of expertise of another person in that field?
Answer: One can estimate the level of expertise of another person in a given field only if one has “seen”, “observed”, or “tasted” the expertise of that another person. I don't know what “accurately” means in this context. Example: I'm acutely aware of the development of mathematics and theoretical physics of the 20th. century. I must have “encountered” several thousands of terms in mathematics and physics during the past 35 years or so. I reiterate, I said “encountered”; it just means vaguely familiar, strongly familiar, familiar to the point of expertise, etc. Nevertheless, it all counts to nearly zero knowledge on my part! I have the knowledge of mathematics that's in the neighborhood of zero (for these subjects). Same with theoretical physics. However, I have an accurate estimate of how much knowledge, say, Witten possesses in theoretical physics or Serre possesses in mathematics! I know how much work they have done in their respective fields (quantitatively). Serre is the last Fields Medalist whose mathematical career itself spans 70 years! Ignoring senility at 97, if Serre recollects everything he ever said or knew of mathematics or wrote on mathematics, that would form a sizeable chunk of mathematics at the end of the 20th century! There is no mathematical work after 1950 that did not see the influence of Jean-Pierre Serre and there is, perhaps, no mathematician who was not influenced by Serre. In every book on algebraic topology, algebraic geometry, algebraic number theory, commutative algebra, homological algebra, several complex variables, and almost anything related to the above, you find results of Serre! There is no meaning to the term Serre's theorem. It is “one of Serre's theorems”. This is the way Lang describes Serre's results (in his Algebra). Alon Amit is one such writer who has fathomed the depth of the works of great mathematicians, though he humbly admits that he is far from understanding their work technically in many cases. His assessment of their intellectual capacity is very accurate. I identify myself with Alon in this respect, though he is very intelligent in mathematics and I know just a piece of math or two.

Name: Rajratna Adsul
Question: Is it possible to write math expressions in normal human language so that everyone will understand it easily without needing any knowledge of math itself beforehand?
Answer: No. This is not possible. It is, however, possible to interpret certain math expressions in normal human language for someone who has some faint idea of the subject in which the equation under consideration occurs. Richard Feynman did just this. The long math expressions in particle scattering are called the S-matrix elements. It is difficult (though not impossible) to build up the total picture of the process unless you set up a clean and clear dictionary between the term of the S-matrix and a step of the physical process in the scattering. Though contemporary physicists criticized Feynman for his oversimplification of the interpretation of such terms, the Feynman diagrams have come down to us as an indispensable tool in physical interpretation of the quantum processes. An ordinary student of quantum mechanics just needs to know what mathematical term represents which step. This dictionary is the so-called Feynman rules which dominate much of quantum field theory. The ubiquitous use of these pictures called Feynman diagrams has given us the philosophy of interpretation of mathematics in a visualizable way. For example, why is there a Dirac δ − function under the integral which represents some process? Here, the Dirac delta function enforces the conservation of momentum in the process. What does the following expression mean: i q 2 − m 2 ? The above is called a propagator and this term represents the transfer or propagation of momentum from one particle to another. Here q is momentum and m is the mass of the particle in the process. Finally, the integral schematically looks like this: ∫ A B C D d x ∫ Here, A,B,C,D are the math terms in the S-matrix of the process. Each of these A,B,C,D has a physical meaning corresponding to the step of the process. In other words, each symbol has a Feynman diagram. We read the terms from right to left, i.e. from D towards A. It means a particle with property D starts to meet at a point x making some interaction C , then going toward some x ′ to meet someone with some energy B and finally going out to infinity with some property A . This is very rough idea but it renders the flavor. Schwinger and Wheeler objected to Feynman for such a classical depiction of quantum processes. But barring rigor, Feynman gave us this beautiful piece of interplay of mathematical expressions and physical ideas. However, the question asks too much. One needs some basic familiarity with math ideas.

Name: Rajratna Adsul
Question: What is more important for someone studying mathematics, understanding something or being able to explain it? Why?
Answer: If you can explain a mathematical idea, you obviously have understood it. But the converse is not true. You have understood an idea, but it does not imply that you can very well explain it. The one who does both is incredible. To explain demands several factors: you explain through speaking or writing. The following is not connected with the question directly. Nearly 20 years back, Roger Penrose visited Pune for a lecture. Pune is a city in Maharashtra nearly 120 km. away from my home. I couldn't attend it as the news reached to me late. Later on, few local newspapers covered this event. They wrote: What Penrose spoke was not audible to the audience even though the subject was interesting such as artificial intelligence and the role of consciousness in quantum gravity. This was the question-answer session and Penrose seemed to just mumble. The hall was packed and it was a cool Saturday morning….. Now that I have watched his videos on YouTube and I don't seem to agree totally with the above verdict. Witten too speaks with unclear matter. Remember, these are first-rate world mathematicians and their intellectual effusion has nothing to do with their knowledge. It is just their personality trait of speaking; this much we can say. As a trivia, I say that Roger Penrose was received by Professor Shashikumar Madhusudan Chitre at the Mumbai airport. Prof. Chitre was one of the world renowned experts in general relativity and, sometime later, I had the golden opportunity to meet him in 2002 at a Mumbai Science Festival. Chitre was a close friend of S.W. Hawking and a classmate of Penrose!
